opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the reason we started with superconductors really comes down to a few things. Coming from quantum computing, that was the platform I knew best. A lot of us on the founding team had spent years working with superconducting circuits, Josephson junctions, dilution fridges, the whole stack. So there was a ton of existing know-how and fabrication infrastructure we could lean on rather than starting from zero.

But beyond familiarity, there's a real physics argument. With a thermodynamic computer, you want devices whose natural dynamics are stochastic, where the noise is a feature, not a bug. And you want to be able to precisely engineer the energy landscape those degrees of freedom live in. Superconducting circuits are fantastic for that. They're very low dissipation, so you have clean, well-characterized dynamics, and the Josephson junction gives you a tunable nonlinearity, so you can shape potentials, couple elements together, and basically program the Hamiltonian you want the system to sample from.

Also, superconducting systems sit in a nice regime where you can dial how much thermal fluctuation versus quantum behavior you get. In quantum computing we spend enormous effort fighting noise and decoherence. Here we flip that on its head: we let the system thermalize and use those fluctuations as the computational resource for things like sampling and probabilistic inference.

So it was a proof-of-concept choice. Show that the core idea of physics-based, noise-native, probabilistic computing works in a clean, controllable platform. The longer-term goal was always to move toward something scalable and room temperature, like more conventional CMOS-compatible approaches, so it can be deployed widely. Superconductors were the place to validate the principles first, then you port the ideas to hardware that can scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a good question, because a lot of people hear "thermodynamic computing" and assume we'd want something warm and noisy, like a room-temperature analog circuit. And actually, long-term, that's where we want to go. But as a starting point, superconductors were the right call for a few reasons.

The first is that we needed a substrate where the physics is extremely well characterized. If you're building a computer that computes with noise, with fluctuations, you need to understand exactly where that noise is coming from and how it couples to your degrees of freedom. Superconducting circuits are probably the best-understood dynamical systems in all of engineering at this point. Decades of work from the quantum computing world, from SQUID magnetometry, from Josephson junction electronics. The Hamiltonians are known, the dissipation channels are known, you can model the thing down to very high fidelity. So we could design a device on paper and be fairly confident it would behave the way we predicted.

The second is tunability. A Josephson junction gives you a nonlinear element whose parameters you can tune in situ with a flux bias. So you can shape the energy landscape of the system dynamically, which is exactly what you want if you're trying to sample from a programmable distribution. You're literally programming the Hamiltonian and letting the thermal bath do the sampling for you. That's hard to do with, say, a transistor-based circuit, where the nonlinearity is kind of baked in.

The third is that low temperature actually gives you control over the noise rather than eliminating it. People assume cryogenic means you're killing the thermal fluctuations, but what you're really doing is setting the temperature as a knob. You can engineer the ratio between your energy scales and kT precisely, so the dynamics sit in the regime where the stochastic contribution is useful rather than overwhelming. And importantly, you're in the classical regime, not quantum. We're not fighting decoherence. We're not trying to maintain fragile superpositions. We're just using the fact that a cold, clean system has a very predictable Langevin dynamics.

And then honestly, there was an opportunistic element. A lot of us came out of the quantum computing world, so we had the fab know-how, the cryogenics, the measurement infrastructure. It was a path where we could get to a working proof of concept quickly and show that the paradigm actually does what the theory says. Once you've demonstrated that, you can start asking: what's the minimal physics we need, and can we get it at room temperature in CMOS? That's the direction we're heading now. But you want to prove the idea in the cleanest possible system first, and for us that was superconductors.

astra-6.text:
Superconducting circuits give you a way to engineer a physical system whose dynamics you can control very precisely. You can design the energy landscape, tune the interactions between different elements, and couple the system to an environment. Those are the ingredients you need if you want to use thermodynamics itself to perform computation.

The key is that noise isn’t simply something you’re trying to eliminate. You want fluctuations to help the system explore possible states, while the energy landscape biases it toward useful answers. Low dissipation is valuable because you want those dynamics to unfold without losing control of them.

There’s also a practical reason: superconducting computing and quantum computing have developed a substantial toolbox for fabricating, controlling, and measuring these circuits. So it’s a useful starting point for testing the idea, even though thermodynamic computing isn’t fundamentally tied to superconductors.

sol-6.1.text:
The appeal of superconductors is that you can engineer a physical system whose dynamics are very close to the mathematical model you want to compute with. You have collective degrees of freedom, like the phase of a superconducting circuit, and you can shape their energy landscape through the circuit design.

For a thermodynamic computer, you’re trying to make those physical dynamics do useful computational work. Instead of treating fluctuations purely as noise to suppress, you want to use them to explore an energy landscape and sample from a distribution. Superconducting circuits give you a way to control the landscape, the interactions, and the coupling to the environment.

There’s also a practical reason: there’s already a substantial engineering toolkit around superconducting circuits. So it’s a compelling starting point for asking whether we can build a programmable machine that computes through its own physical relaxation and fluctuations.
